notes:
Now let me compile all the research into a verse-by-verse commentary. I'll draw from the substantial material gathered from Enduring Word, Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary, Precept Austin, MacLaren, and the Expositor's Bible.

---

# 1 Samuel 18 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## v. 1 — "After David had finished speaking with Saul, the souls of Jonathan and David were knit together, and Jonathan loved him as himself."

This verse follows directly from the conversation in 1 Samuel 17:57–58 where David — still holding Goliath's head — answered Saul's questions about his identity. As David spoke, Jonathan (Saul's son and crown prince) heard David's heart and his faith in the living God, and recognised a kindred spirit. The Hebrew verb translated "knit" (*qashar*) means literally "bound" or "tied together," conveying an inseparable bond. The same word is used in Genesis 44:30 of Jacob's life being "bound up" with Benjamin's — a love so deep that one's life depends on the other's well-being. Jonathan and David were approximately the same age, both bold warriors, both men of great faith; what they shared in common — a real relationship with the LORD — was bigger than any rivalry over the throne. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/) · [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-18-commentary) · [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/18.htm)

Ellicott notes that Jonathan was "the type of a true warrior... chivalrous and generous — utterly free from jealousy." He adds that what won Jonathan's heart was not just David's bravery but his "sublime faith, his perfect childlike trust in the 'Glorious Arm' of the Lord." [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/18.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary says these "kindred spirits had so much in common that… an intense feeling of admiration grew up in the young warrior's heart, and a friendship was the result which ranks among the purest and noblest examples of true manly affection." [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/18.htm)

Several sources address the question of whether the love between Jonathan and David was homosexual. Precept Austin notes that the Hebrew verb *'ahab* ("love") is never used in the OT to describe homosexual desire or activity; instead the OT uses *yada* ("to know") for sexual relationships, and *yada* is never used of Jonathan and David. [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-18-commentary) · Enduring Word adds that the Bible does not "condemn real love between men, only a sexual relationship between men." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

---

## v. 2 — "And from that day Saul kept David with him and did not let him return to his father's house."

From that day forward, David was no longer a part-time court musician who returned to shepherd his father's sheep (1 Samuel 17:15). Saul, recognising David's military potential, took him permanently into his service. Gill notes that previously David "only served as a musician to him… and in the intervals kept his father's sheep," but now Saul "would not suffer him to attend such business any longer, since he was not only to become a courtier… but to marry his daughter, according to the declaration he had made." [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-18.html)

The Pulpit Commentary observes that "bent solely on war, Saul gladly took so promising a young soldier as David to be one of his bodyguard." [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## v. 3 — "Then Jonathan made a covenant with David because he loved him as himself."

The covenant was a solemn bond of mutual friendship. Ellicott explains: "The son of the first Hebrew king recognised in David a kindred spirit. They were one in their God, in their faith, in their devotion to the Divine will." He draws a parallel to Jonathan's own words in 1 Samuel 14:6 — "It may be that the Lord will work for us: for there is no restraint to the Lord to save by many or by few" — seeing the same sublime faith in David that Jonathan himself possessed. [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/18.htm)

Gill writes that this was "a covenant of friendship; entered into a solemn agreement to keep up and maintain a cordial respect to each other, and to support each other's interest both in life and after death, whoever was the survivor." [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-18.html)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that this covenant was not made immediately but developed over time as "the love which began with admiration of David's prowess grew deeper and more confirmed by constant intercourse." [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## v. 4 — "And Jonathan removed the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his tunic, his sword, his bow, and his belt."

Jonathan's gifts were profoundly symbolic. The *me'il* (robe) was the garment of a prince or wealthy person; the military garments, sword, bow, and belt were the prince's war-equipment. By clothing David in his own princely attire, Jonathan was effectively saying, "You will be the next king of Israel. God's hand is on you and these rightfully belong to you." Jonathan surrendered his own claim to the throne in recognition of God's choice. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/) · [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/18.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary adds: "In thus clothing David in his own princely equipments Jonathan was showing his friend the greatest personal honour (Esther 6:8), and such a gift is still highly esteemed in the East." [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/18.htm)

Gill notes: "As a token of his hearty love and true friendship, and that David might appear at court not in the habit of a shepherd, but in that of a prince." [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-18.html)

---

## v. 5 — "So David marched out and prospered in everything Saul sent him to do, and Saul set him over the men of war. And this was pleasing in the sight of all the people, and of Saul's officers as well."

This verse is a summary statement covering an extended period. David went on military expeditions and "behaved himself wisely" (the Hebrew verb can mean both "act prudently" and "prosper"). The Pulpit Commentary notes: "It was only gradually that David's fame became so great as to rouse all the worst feelings in Saul's mind." David's promotion to "over the men of war" was a remarkable rise for a young man perhaps in his early twenties — now essentially a general in Israel's army. Yet even Saul's own servants (those closest and most loyal to the king) accepted and approved of David, showing that David did not gain favour through flattery or political maneuvering but through genuine godly character. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/) · [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/18.htm)

MacLaren notes that this verse "anticipates 1 Samuel 18:13–16" and is "the last verse of a section which interrupts the even flow of the story, and which is absent from the Septuagint." [MacLaren](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/maclaren/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## vv. 6–7 — "As the troops were returning home… the women came out of all the cities of Israel to meet King Saul with singing and dancing… 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his tens of thousands.'"

When David returned from a decisive victory over the Philistines (not necessarily the Goliath combat alone, but likely a subsequent campaign), the women greeted the returning army in traditional Eastern fashion with dancing, tambourines, and antiphonal singing — two groups answering each other. The Pulpit Commentary explains: "It was this alternate singing which led to the psalms being composed in parallel sentences, and not in metre; and we from the temple service have inherited our method of chanting antiphonally." The women's song was a typical Hebrew parallelism honouring both heroes, but the comparison — Saul's thousands versus David's ten thousands — was explosive. [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/18.htm)

The Expositor's Bible notes the coarseness of the compliment: "To honour David as more ready to incur risk and sacrifice for his country… would have been worthy of women… but to make the standard of compliment the number of lives destroyed, the amount of bloodshed, indicated surely a coarseness of feeling, characteristic of a somewhat barbarous age." [Expositor's Bible](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## vv. 8–9 — "And Saul was furious and resented this song… 'What more can he have but the kingdom?' And from that day forward Saul kept a jealous eye on David."

Saul's reaction reveals his deep insecurity. Enduring Word suggests that Saul was haunted by Samuel's pronouncement that the LORD had rejected him from being king (1 Samuel 15:28). His guilty conscience made him constantly scan the horizon for his replacement. The song confirmed his worst fears. Saul could have rejoiced in his subordinate's success, but instead he overreacted: "Now what more can he have but the kingdom?" [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

The Hebrew for "kept a jealous eye" (Gill: "eyed David") means Saul watched David with a "sour, ill-natured look… with an evil, spiteful, malicious, and envious eye; or he diligently watched and observed all his motions and actions, whether they tended to disloyalty and treason." [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-18.html)

MacLaren calls this "the first stage" of Saul's tragic descent: "There are few men, holding high places in any walk of life, who could have stood such a comparison without wincing… Poor Saul had to drink the bitter cup, which all who love the sweet draught of popular applause have sooner or later to taste." [MacLaren](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/maclaren/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## v. 10 — "The next day a spirit of distress sent from God came upon Saul, and he prophesied inside the house while David played the harp as usual. Now Saul was holding a spear."

The "distressing spirit from God" was first mentioned in 1 Samuel 16:14. It was permitted by the LORD after His Spirit departed from Saul. Enduring Word explains that "prophesied" is a poor translation here; the Hebrew grammar can refer to "idle ravings" as well as genuine prophecy. Saul "simply babbled like a man not in his right mind." Clarke is quoted: "He was beside himself; made prayers, supplications, and incoherent imprecations." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

Gill similarly notes: "Either really, delivering out divine songs, as the prophets did… or he feigned himself a prophet, mimicking their motions and gestures; or, as the Targum, acted like a mad man, or a fool, uttering foolish words, and using ridiculous gestures." [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-18.html)

The contrast is vivid: David held a harp to minister; Saul held a spear to murder. David's same hands that had killed Goliath now played music in humble service. The same music ministry that once soothed Saul (1 Samuel 16:23) now had no effect because Saul's heart had hardened further. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

---

## v. 11 — "And he hurled it, thinking, 'I will pin David to the wall.' But David eluded him twice."

This was not an accident — Saul's intention was lethal. Yet David escaped twice, which Enduring Word calls "perhaps the most remarkable word in this chapter." After the first spear-throw, David came back and played music again, knowing the danger. David refused to pick up the spear and throw it back: "David was determined to leave the situation in God's hands, and not take the throne himself. God would have to take care of Saul because David wouldn't do it." If David had retaliated, he might still have become king — but not the king God destined him to be. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

MacLaren writes: "Envy, allowed to have its way, becomes murderous. Let us suppress its beginning. A tiger pup can be held in and its claws cut, but a full-grown tiger cannot." [MacLaren](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/maclaren/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## v. 12 — "So Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with David but had departed from Saul."

Saul's fear was spiritual at root. By all outward measures Saul had the throne, the army, and the spears — yet he feared David because of God's presence with the young man. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the contrast between the LORD being with David and departed from Saul was the real source of Saul's terror. [Pulpit Commentary](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_samuel/18.htm) · [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

Gill writes that Saul feared David "lest the time was drawing near that the kingdom should be rent from him, and given to David." [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-18.html)

---

## vv. 13–14 — "Therefore Saul sent David away and gave him command of a thousand men. David led the troops out to battle and back, and he continued to prosper in all his ways, because the LORD was with him."

Saul's removal of David from court was dressed as a promotion but was in truth banishment — "under pretence of doing him honour, when it was in effect only to rid himself of the object of his envy" (Clarke, quoted in Enduring Word). Saul hoped David would fall in battle. Yet David prospered precisely because the LORD was with him. The phrase "went out and came in" is a Hebrew idiom for conducting successful military operations. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/) · [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-18.html)

For David to "behave wisely" while under attack was remarkable. Enduring Word notes: "It isn't easy to behave wisely when spears are being thrown at you. It isn't easy to behave wisely when you are put out of the palace. It isn't easy to behave wisely when you have powerful and determined enemies." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

---

## vv. 15–16 — "When Saul saw that David was very successful, he was afraid of him. But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he was leading them out to battle and back."

Saul's fear intensified. The Hebrew word in v.15 is stronger than in v.12. MacLaren describes it as "a pathetic picture of the gradual creeping over a strong man of a nameless terror. Ever-thickening folds of cold dread, like a wet mist, wrap a soul once bright and energetic." Meanwhile, David's popularity grew with all the people — "all Israel and Judah loved David." The verb is singular, emphasising that each individual loved him. [MacLaren](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/maclaren/1_samuel/18.htm) · [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-18.html)

The Expositor's Bible notes the tragic contrast: "Two souls stand side by side for a moment on the same platform, with the same divine goodness and love encircling them, and the one steadily rises, while the other steadily sinks." [Expositor's Bible](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## v. 17 — "Then Saul said to David, 'Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you in marriage. Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD's battles.' But Saul was thinking, 'I need not raise my hand against him; let the hand of the Philistines be against him.'"

Saul had promised his daughter to the man who killed Goliath (1 Samuel 17:25). Now he seemingly made good on the promise, but with a hidden agenda. Enduring Word calls this "a trap" — Saul's public kindness masked private murderous intent. He hoped the Philistines would do what he could not. This is Saul's "spiritually powerless" manipulation; his hidden agendas all failed because David's humble heart and God's protection kept him safe. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

The Expositor's Bible notes that if Saul had genuinely promised his daughter, "there was no reason at the time why he should not have kept his promise." The delayed fulfilment suggests the original promise may have been an "unauthorised rumour" reported to David, or that David's humble origins made an immediate royal marriage inappropriate. [Expositor's Bible](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## v. 18 — "And David said to Saul, 'Who am I, and what is my family or my father's clan in Israel, that I should become the son-in-law of the king?'"

David's response reveals genuine humility — not false modesty. He was not out-maneuvering Saul; he had no idea of Saul's murderous schemes. His humble heart was his protection. Enduring Word notes: "David simply had a humble heart before the LORD, and God protected him against Saul's manipulation." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

Ellicott calls this response evidence that David was "not ambitious or self-seeking." [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## v. 19 — "So when it was time to give Saul's daughter Merab to David, she was given in marriage to Adriel of Meholah."

Saul broke his promise. David later regarded this as a cruel wrong (2 Samuel 3:13). The Expositor's Bible notes: "Saul went back on his promise to give David his older daughter… The next stage in the career of jealousy is to ally itself with cunning, under the pretence of great generosity." [Expositor's Bible](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## vv. 20–21 — "Now Saul's daughter Michal loved David, and when this was reported to Saul, it pleased him. 'I will give her to David,' Saul thought, 'so that she may be a snare to him, and the hand of the Philistines may be against him.'"

Saul's younger daughter Michal genuinely loved David. Saul saw this as another opportunity for his plots. He intended Michal to be "a snare" — perhaps by the dangerous dowry he would demand, or by using her as a spy within David's household. Ellicott comments that Saul's dark plot — using his own daughter's love to destroy a man — may later have suggested to David the means by which he got rid of Uriah the Hittite (2 Samuel 11). [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/18.htm)

Enduring Word notes that though Michal loved David, she was "not really attracted to David's heart for the LORD" — as her later contempt for David's worship (2 Samuel 6:16) would reveal. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

---

## vv. 22–23 — "Then Saul ordered his servants, 'Speak to David privately…' But when Saul's servants relayed these words to David, he replied, 'Does it seem trivial in your sight to be the son-in-law of the king? I am a poor man and lightly esteemed.'"

Saul used his servants to flatter David and pressure him into the marriage. David's reply was again humble — he was a poor man who could not afford the customary dowry. This was not false humility but honest acknowledgment of his social standing. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/) · [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-18.html)

---

## v. 25 — "Saul replied, 'Say to David, "The king desires no other dowry but a hundred Philistine foreskins as revenge on his enemies."' But Saul intended to cause David's death at the hands of the Philistines."

The dowry demand was both grotesque and calculated. Saul thought such a dangerous mission would surely get David killed. The request for foreskins proved the Philistines were killed (unlike scalps or heads, which could be faked or ambiguous). The Expositor's Bible calls Saul's behaviour increasingly black: "Saul was not merely trifling with the heart and happiness of his child, but he was deliberately sacrificing both to his vile passion." [Expositor's Bible](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/1_samuel/18.htm) · [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

---

## vv. 26–27 — "When the servants reported these terms to David, he was pleased to become the king's son-in-law… David and his men went out and killed two hundred Philistines. He brought their foreskins and presented them as payment in full…"

David was pleased — not because he was ambitious, but because the prospect of the alliance spurred him on. He exceeded Saul's demand, bringing 200 foreskins instead of 100, answering manipulation with humble, generous service. Enduring Word says: "David had such a pure, humble heart that he seemed to be blind to Saul's manipulation and cunning. A simple man can survive amid such treachery when God is with him." [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

Ellicott comments on the brutal reality: "The savage, half-barbarous state of the age… comes prominently into view when we reflect upon the ferocious cruelty of such an offer being made and accepted." [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## vv. 28–29 — "When Saul realized that the LORD was with David and that his daughter Michal loved David, he grew even more afraid of David. So from then on Saul was David's enemy."

Saul saw and knew — with certainty — that the LORD was with David. Yet this knowledge did not lead him to repentance; it only increased his fear and solidified his enmity. Gill notes that Saul also realised Michal loved David and "therefore could entertain no hope of making use of her as an instrument of his ruin, but, on the contrary, would… betray the designs of her father against him." [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-18.html)

Ellicott writes: "The success of the last savage enterprise, and the return of David with his ghastly spoils, filled the unhappy king with dismay… Saul felt that all that David undertook prospered — that surely another and a higher Power was helping him. So his fear grew… and the paroxysms of jealous hatred deepened into a lifelong enmity." [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## v. 30 — "Every time the Philistine commanders came out for battle, David was more successful than all of Saul's officers, so that his name was highly esteemed."

The chapter ends with David's reputation continuing to rise, even as Saul's hatred deepened. David "behaved himself more wisely than all the servants of Saul" — the same Hebrew root used throughout the chapter for wise/prudent/successful conduct. The Expositor's Bible summarises the broader lesson: at this period, David was at his "most blameless and beautiful" — "the object of unmerited hatred, the victim of atrocious plots… yet cherishing no trace of bitter feeling, dreaming of no violent project of relief, but going out and in with perfect loyalty, and straining every nerve to prove himself a laborious, faithful, and useful servant of the master who loathed him." [Expositor's Bible](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/1_samuel/18.htm) · [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

Ellicott notes that David had "regarded himself as lightly esteemed" (v.23) but now God made him "highly esteemed" — a reversal that is a hallmark of God's way with the humble. [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

## Summary of Denominationally Distinct Readings

While the traditional reading of 1 Samuel 18 is broadly consistent across Protestant traditions, I can note the following distinct emphases found in the sources consulted:

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises the spiritual warfare dimension — Saul's "distressing spirit" as a real spiritual affliction permitted by God, and David's music as genuine spiritual ministry that once brought deliverance. Highlights David's refusal to retaliate as a model of surrendering one's destiny to God rather than taking matters into one's own hands. The application is strongly personal and devotional, urging believers to trust God's timing. [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-18/)

**Baptist / Older Evangelical (Gill, MacLaren, Spurgeon referenced in Precept Austin):** Gill's Exposition (18th-century Baptist) is characteristically thorough on the Hebrew text and historical detail. MacLaren (19th-century Baptist preacher) traces the psychological and spiritual descent of Saul in three stages, with strong moral application about the danger of unchecked envy. Spurgeon (quoted in Precept Austin) praised Jonathan as "the brave young soldier" who "naturally admired the youthful warrior." [Gill](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-18.html) · [MacLaren](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/maclaren/1_samuel/18.htm) · [Precept Austin](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-18-commentary)

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott's commentary (19th-century Anglican bishop) draws careful literary and historical observations, noting for instance that Ellicott uniquely raises the question of whether Saul's plot against David later suggested to David the method of disposing of Uriah (2 Samuel 11) — a moral-theological connection not made in other commentaries consulted. [Ellicott](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/18.htm)

**Reformed / Presbyterian (Expositor's Bible — W. G. Blaikie):** Emphasises God's sovereign purpose in David's sufferings as "hard discipline and salutary training for the office to which he was to be raised," drawing a parallel to Christ: "Even our blessed Lord, David's antitype, 'though He was a Son, yet learned He obedience by the things which He suffered.'" The Expositor's Bible also stresses the lesson that the same seeds of evil were in David's heart as in Saul's — only grace and the Spirit's restraining power kept David from the same ruin. [Expositor's Bible](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/1_samuel/18.htm)

---

**Note on traditions not covered:** Due to search limitations, I was unable to access dedicated Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Methodist/Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), or NET Bible notes (netbible.org) pages. The sources actually retrieved represent Pentecostal/Charismatic, Baptist, Reformed/Presbyterian, Anglican, and broad Evangelical traditions.
